UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE WEEKLY CLAIMS

  SEASONALLY ADJUSTED DATA

In the week ending November 7, the advance figure for seasonally adjusted initial claims was 200,000, an increase of
9,000 from the previous week's revised level. The previous week's level was revised up by 2,000 from 189,000 to
191,000. The 4-week moving average was 195,250, unchanged from the previous week's revised average. The previous
week's average was revised up by 500 from 194,750 to 195,250.

The advance seasonally adjusted insured unemployment rate was 1.1 percent for the week ending October 31,
unchanged from the previous week's unrevised rate. The advance number for seasonally adjusted insured
unemployment during the week ending October 31 was 1,697,000, a decrease of 20,000 from the previous week's
revised level. The previous week's level was revised down by 1,000 from 1,718,000 to 1,717,000. The 4-week moving
average was 1,707,750, a decrease of 1,500 from the previous week's revised average. The previous week's average was
revised down by 250 from 1,709,500 to 1,709,250.

[Page 2]
UNADJUSTED DATA

The advance number of actual initial claims under state programs, unadjusted, totaled 206,982 in the week ending
November 7, an increase of 28,870 (or 16.2 percent) from the previous week. The seasonal factors had expected an
increase of 19,663 (or 11.0 percent) from the previous week. There were 238,729 initial claims in the comparable week
in 2025.

The advance unadjusted insured unemployment rate was 1.0 percent during the week ending October 31, unchanged
from the prior week. The advance unadjusted level of insured unemployment in state programs totaled 1,503,556, an
increase of 10,117 (or 0.7 percent) from the preceding week. The seasonal factors had expected an increase of 27,466
(or 1.8 percent) from the previous week. A year earlier the rate was 1.1 percent and the volume was 1,720,202.




The total number of continued weeks claimed for benefits in all programs for the week ending October 24 was
1,517,924, an increase of 10,207 from the previous week. There were 1,768,408 weekly claims filed for benefits in all
programs in the comparable week in 2025.

No state was triggered "on" the Extended Benefits program during the week ending October 24.

Initial claims for UI benefits filed by former Federal civilian employees totaled 585 in the week ending October 31, an
increase of 33 from the prior week. There were 407 initial claims filed by newly discharged veterans, an increase of 60
from the preceding week.

There were 5,327 continued weeks claimed filed by former Federal civilian employees the week ending October 24, an
increase of 199 from the previous week. Newly discharged veterans claiming benefits totaled 5,008, an increase of 67
from the prior week.

The highest insured unemployment rates in the week ending October 24 were in New Jersey (2.0), Washington (1.9),
Massachusetts (1.8), California (1.7), Puerto Rico (1.6), Nevada (1.5), Oregon (1.5), Rhode Island (1.5), New York (1.4),
Illinois (1.3), and the Virgin Islands (1.3).

The largest increases in initial claims for the week ending October 31 were in Illinois (+728), Indiana (+655),
Washington (+647), Missouri (+394), and Oregon (+365), while the largest decreases were in New York (-1,524),
Texas (-1,481), Kentucky (-805), Florida (-722), and Michigan (-378).

TECHNICAL NOTES

This news release presents the weekly unemployment insurance (UI) claims reported by each state's unemployment
insurance program offices. These claims may be used for monitoring workload volume, assessing state program
operations and for assessing labor market conditions. States initially report claims directly taken by the state liable for the
benefit payments, regardless of where the claimant who filed the claim resided. These are the basis for the advance initial
claims and continued claims reported each week. These data come from ETA 538, Advance Weekly Initial and
Continued Claims Report. The following week initial claims and continued claims are revised based on a second
reporting by states that reflect the claimants by state of residence. These data come from the ETA 539, Weekly Claims
and Extended Benefits Trigger Data Report.

A. Initial Claims

An initial claim is a claim filed by an unemployed individual after a separation from an employer. The claimant requests
a determination of basic eligibility for the UI program. When an initial claim is filed with a state, certain programmatic
activities take place and these result in activity counts including the count of initial claims. The count of U.S. initial
claims for unemployment insurance is a leading economic indicator because it is an indication of emerging labor market
conditions in the country. However, these are weekly administrative data which are difficult to seasonally adjust, making
the series subject to some volatility.

B. Continued Weeks Claimed

A person who has already filed an initial claim and who has experienced a week of unemployment then files a continued
claim to claim benefits for that week of unemployment. On a weekly basis, continued claims are also referred to as
insured unemployment, as continued claims reflect a good approximation of the current number of insured unemployed
workers filing for UI benefits. The count of U.S. continued weeks claimed is also a good indicator of labor market
conditions. While continued claims are not a leading indicator (they roughly coincide with economic cycles at their peaks
and lag at cycle troughs), they provide confirming evidence of the direction of the U.S. economy.

C. Seasonal Adjustments and Annual Revisions

Over the course of a year, the weekly changes in the levels of initial claims and continued claims undergo regularly
occurring fluctuations. These fluctuations may result from seasonal changes in weather, major holidays, the opening and
closing of schools, or other similar events. Because these seasonal events follow a more or less regular pattern each year,
their influence on the level of a series can be tempered by adjusting for regular seasonal variation. These adjustments
make trend and cycle developments easier to spot. At the beginning of each calendar year, the Bureau of Labor Statistics
provides the Employment and Training Administration (ETA) with a set of seasonal factors to apply to the unadjusted
data during that year. Concurrent with the implementation and release of the new seasonal factors, ETA incorporates
revisions to the UI claims historical series caused by updates to the unadjusted data. For further questions on the seasonal
adjustment methodology, please see the official release page for the UI claims seasonal adjustment factors or contact
BLS directly through the Local Area Unemployment Statistics web contact form.

unemployment during the week ending October 31 was 1,697,000, a decrease of 20,000 from the previous week's

UNADJUSTED DATA

The advance number of actual initial claims under state programs, unadjusted, totaled 206,982 in the week ending
November 7, an increase of 28,870 (or 16.2 percent) from the previous week. The seasonal factors had expected an
increase of 19,663 (or 11.0 percent) from the previous week. There were 238,729 initial claims in the comparable week
in 2025.

The advance unadjusted insured unemployment rate was 1.0 percent during the week ending October 31, unchanged
from the prior week. The advance unadjusted level of insured unemployment in state programs totaled 1,503,556, an
increase of 10,117 (or 0.7 percent) from the preceding week. The seasonal factors had expected an increase of 27,466
(or 1.8 percent) from the previous week. A year earlier the rate was 1.1 percent and the volume was 1,720,202.




The total number of continued weeks claimed for benefits in all programs for the week ending October 24 was
1,517,924, an increase of 10,207 from the previous week. There were 1,768,408 weekly claims filed for benefits in all
programs in the comparable week in 2025.

No state was triggered "on" the Extended Benefits program during the week ending October 24.

Initial claims for UI benefits filed by former Federal civilian employees totaled 585 in the week ending October 31, an
increase of 33 from the prior week. There were 407 initial claims filed by newly discharged veterans, an increase of 60
from the preceding week.

There were 5,327 continued weeks claimed filed by former Federal civilian employees the week ending October 24, an
increase of 199 from the previous week. Newly discharged veterans claiming benefits totaled 5,008, an increase of 67
from the prior week.

TECHNICAL NOTES

This news release presents the weekly unemployment insurance (UI) claims reported by each state's unemployment
insurance program offices. These claims may be used for monitoring workload volume, assessing state program
operations and for assessing labor market conditions. States initially report claims directly taken by the state liable for the
benefit payments, regardless of where the claimant who filed the claim resided. These are the basis for the advance initial
claims and continued claims reported each week. These data come from ETA 538, Advance Weekly Initial and
Continued Claims Report. The following week initial claims and continued claims are revised based on a second
reporting by states that reflect the claimants by state of residence. These data come from the ETA 539, Weekly Claims
and Extended Benefits Trigger Data Report.

A. Initial Claims

An initial claim is a claim filed by an unemployed individual after a separation from an employer. The claimant requests
a determination of basic eligibility for the UI program. When an initial claim is filed with a state, certain programmatic
activities take place and these result in activity counts including the count of initial claims. The count of U.S. initial
claims for unemployment insurance is a leading economic indicator because it is an indication of emerging labor market
conditions in the country. However, these are weekly administrative data which are difficult to seasonally adjust, making
the series subject to some volatility.

B. Continued Weeks Claimed

A person who has already filed an initial claim and who has experienced a week of unemployment then files a continued
claim to claim benefits for that week of unemployment. On a weekly basis, continued claims are also referred to as
insured unemployment, as continued claims reflect a good approximation of the current number of insured unemployed
workers filing for UI benefits. The count of U.S. continued weeks claimed is also a good indicator of labor market
conditions. While continued claims are not a leading indicator (they roughly coincide with economic cycles at their peaks
and lag at cycle troughs), they provide confirming evidence of the direction of the U.S. economy.

C. Seasonal Adjustments and Annual Revisions

Over the course of a year, the weekly changes in the levels of initial claims and continued claims undergo regularly
occurring fluctuations. These fluctuations may result from seasonal changes in weather, major holidays, the opening and
closing of schools, or other similar events. Because these seasonal events follow a more or less regular pattern each year,
their influence on the level of a series can be tempered by adjusting for regular seasonal variation. These adjustments
make trend and cycle developments easier to spot. At the beginning of each calendar year, the Bureau of Labor Statistics
provides the Employment and Training Administration (ETA) with a set of seasonal factors to apply to the unadjusted
data during that year. Concurrent with the implementation and release of the new seasonal factors, ETA incorporates
revisions to the UI claims historical series caused by updates to the unadjusted data. For further questions on the seasonal
adjustment methodology, please see the official release page for the UI claims seasonal adjustment factors or contact
BLS directly through the Local Area Unemployment Statistics web contact form.

**技術注記**

この発表は、州の失業保険担当機関が報告した毎週の失業保険申請を示す。申請統計は事務量の把握、州制度の運用評価、労働市場の評価に使える。まず、給付の支払い義務を負う州が、申請者の居住地にかかわらず直接受け付けた申請を報告する。毎週報告する新規・継続申請の速報は、このデータをもとに作成する。原資料はETA 538「週間新規・継続申請速報報告」。翌週、州が申請者の居住州別に行う第2回報告をもとに新規・継続申請を改定する。原資料はETA 539「週間申請・延長給付発動データ報告」。

**A. 新規申請**

新規申請は、離職後に失業者が提出する申請で、失業保険の基本受給資格の判定を求めるもの。州に新規申請が提出されると制度上の所定の事務処理が行われ、その処理件数の中に新規申請件数が含まれる。米国の新規失業保険申請件数は、労働市場の変化の兆しを示す先行指標。週次の行政データは季節調整が難しく、変動が生じやすい。

**B. 申請延べ給付週数**

新規申請済みの人が失業した状態で1週間を過ごした場合、その週の給付を受けるため継続申請を行う。週次の継続申請は、失業保険の給付を申請する被保険失業者数のよい近似になるため、「被保険失業」とも呼ばれる。米国の申請延べ給付週数も労働市場を把握する指標。景気の山とはおおむね同時、谷には遅行し、米国経済の方向を裏付ける。

**C. 季節調整と年次改定**

新規申請と継続申請の水準は年間を通じ、週ごとに規則的な変動がある。季節による天候の変化、主な祝日、学校の始業・終業などが理由になり得る。こうした季節的な事象は毎年おおむね規則的なため、規則的な季節変動を調整すれば系列の水準への影響を抑えられる。調整により傾向や景気循環の変化を見極めやすくなる。年初に労働統計局が雇用訓練局（ETA）へ、その年の調整前データに適用する季節係数を提供する。新しい係数の適用・公表と同時に、ETAは調整前データの更新による失業保険申請の過去系列の改定を反映する。調整方法の質問は[季節調整係数の公表ページ](https://www.bls.gov/lau/seasonal-adjustment-for-weekly-unemployment-insurance-claims.htm)または[労働統計局の地域失業統計フォーム](https://data.bls.gov/forms/lau.htm?/lau/laucont.htm)へ。

[週間申請の過去資料](https://oui.doleta.gov/unemploy/claims_arch.asp)・[週間申請データ](https://oui.doleta.gov/unemploy/claims.asp)。

労働省の報道資料は[労働省サイト](http://www.dol.gov/)で閲覧できる。同省の[合理的配慮リソースセンター](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/oasam/civil-rights-center/internal/reasonable-accomodations-resource-center)は情報・文書を点字や大活字などの代替形式に変換する。代替形式の依頼は音声電話または連邦リレーで受け付ける。
